Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the material gathered.

# Psalm 78:25–48 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 25: *Man ate the bread of angels; He sent them food in abundance.*

The Hebrew phrase is literally "bread of the mighty ones" (*lechem abirim*). The LXX and Vulgate render it "angels' bread," and most traditional commentators accept this. The Pulpit Commentary explains it may mean either actual food on which angels subsist, or food supplied by angelic ministration and derived from their dwelling-place — adding that "it cannot be laid down dogmatically that angels require no food." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Ellicott notes an alternative view: some explain it after Job 24:22 and 34:30 as "lordly food, such as nobles eat," but concedes that in connection with "food from heaven," the popular idea of angels' food "which poetry reluctantly gives up may be retained." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm)

Gill catalogs multiple interpretations: it could mean food prepared by the ministry of angels, food that descended from the habitation of angels (so the Targum), food of such excellence that it was fit for angels, or (following Cocceius) "bread of the mighty God — Father, Son, and Spirit — by whom this food was prepared and given." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/78.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) emphasizes the contrast: "Their dark sin is set against the white background of God's goodness… He gave them and kept giving them bread of heaven and angels' food, and they ate to the full." He also notes John 6:31, where those whom Jesus fed quoted this psalm — "in quoting this psalm to Jesus, they fulfilled it in a negative way, showing the same ingratitude and willingness to test God that Israel showed in the wilderness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

Calvin (Reformed) remarks that "it was the basest ingratitude to scorn and reject the heavenly food, which, so to speak, associated them with angels." He explains that the manna is called "bread of the mighty" to reprove the people's "twofold ingratitude" — they despised not only common food produced from the ground, "but also the bread of angels." (https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment2/v1.0/harry/comm_vol10/htm/xiii.v.htm)

Spurgeon (Baptist): "The delicacies of kings were outdone, for the dainties of angels were supplied. Bread of the mighty ones fell on feeble man.… It was not for the priests, or the princes, that the manna fell; but for all the nation, for every man, woman, and child in the camp." He adds a gospel application: "Gospel provisions deserve every praise that we can heap upon them; they are free, full, and preeminent." (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php)

---

## v. 26: *He stirred the east wind from the heavens and drove the south wind by His might.*

The Pulpit Commentary observes that "here, again, tradition seems to speak. The narrative in the Pentateuch has only, 'There went forth a wind from the Lord' (Numbers 11:31)." The psalmist adds the detail of east and south winds. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Ellicott notes these were "probably the very winds that brought the flights of quails, and not merely poetical details," pointing readers to Smith's Biblical Dictionary on "Quails." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) explain that "east and south belong together: it was a south-east wind from the Aelanitic Gulf." The verb *yassea* ("He caused to depart, set out") is taken from Numbers 11:31. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 27: *He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.*

The Pulpit Commentary notes the expression "rained flesh" echoes Exodus 16:4 ("I will rain bread from heaven") and Genesis 19:24. "As dust" means "as thick as dust" (Prayer Book Version). It adds that the quails lay "as it were two cubits high" for a day's journey around each encampment (Numbers 11:31). The phrase "as the sand of the sea" is "the commonest image of multiplicity" (Genesis 22:17, etc.). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Spurgeon makes no separate note on this verse beyond the context. Guzik (Enduring Word) references Numbers 11:31-33 for the historical basis.

---

## v. 28: *He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.*

The Pulpit Commentary explains that the quails "covered the camp" (Exodus 16:13) and extended round it on every side (Numbers 11:31). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

The image is of God bringing the birds right to where the people were — making the provision unmistakably miraculous and leaving them without excuse.

---

## v. 29: *So they ate and were well filled, for He gave them what they craved.*

The Pulpit Commentary renders "well filled" as "sated" (comp. Numbers 11:19-20). The phrase "their own desire" is more literally "their own lust — that they lusted after" (so the Revised Version). There is an ironic tone: God granted what they craved, but the granting itself becomes a form of judgment. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Guzik captures the irony: "Israel was well filled, but not with good quail meat in their stomachs. God gave them their own desire, but because their craving was rooted in their self-will, the result was not good." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

---

## v. 30: *Yet before they had filled their desire, with the food still in their mouths,*

The Pulpit Commentary renders the KJV's "They were not estranged from their lust" as meaning "their lust was not yet satiated — they were still indulging it. The meat was yet in their mouths, still undergoing mastication, when…" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

This heightens the dramatic suddenness of the judgment that follows. The very moment of indulgence becomes the moment of wrath.

---

## v. 31: *God's anger flared against them, and He put to death their strongest and subdued the young men of Israel.*

The Pulpit Commentary references Numbers 11:33: "While the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled against the people, and the Lord smote the people with a very great plague." "The fattest of them" (KJV) means the strongest and healthiest; the "chosen men" (KJV) are "the young men" or "ripened youths" (Cheyne). The Pulpit Commentary adds that "here, again, the author adds touches which he has not obtained from the Pentateuch." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Guzik: "God gave a disobedient and rebellious Israel all they desired and craved, and the quail turned to a plague of judgment among them." This is the event at Kibroth-hattaavah ("graves of craving," Numbers 11:34). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

---

## v. 32: *In spite of all this, they kept on sinning; despite His wonderful works, they did not believe.*

Keil & Delitzsch note that when the poet says "in spite of all this" they went on sinning, he has chiefly before his mind "the outbreak of 'fat' rebelliousness after the return of the spies," comparing Psalm 78:32 with Numbers 14:11. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

The central indictment returns: unbelief. As Spurgeon stated on v. 22, this "is the master sin, the crying sin… it is in itself evil and the parent of evils." (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php)

---

## v. 33: *So He ended their days in futility, and their years in sudden terror.*

Keil & Delitzsch refer this to the judgment pronounced in Numbers 14:28-34 — that all who came out of Egypt from twenty years old and upward would die in the wilderness. "Their life devoted to death vanished from that time onwards *bahebel*, in breath-like instability, and *babbehalah*, in undurable precipitancy." The Hebrew creates "an expressive play of words." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 34: *When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.*

Keil & Delitzsch explain: "When now a special judgment suddenly and violently thinned the generation that otherwise was dying off, as in Numbers 21:6… then they inquired after Him, they again sought His favour." The repentance, however, was short-lived and shallow. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 35: *And they remembered that God was their Rock, that God Most High was their Redeemer.*

Keil & Delitzsch note that "those who were still preserved in the midst of this dying again remembered the God who had proved Himself to be a 'Rock' (Deuteronomy 32:15, 18…)." The titles "Rock" (*tsur*) and "Redeemer" (*goel*) evoke God's steadfastness and His act of redemption from Egypt. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 36: *But they deceived Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues.*

The psalmist exposes the superficiality of their repentance. Their words of devotion were flattery and falsehood. The Pulpit Commentary and Keil both frame this as the contrast between outward confession and inward reality.

---

## v. 37: *Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.*

The heart (inner disposition) did not match the tongue (outward profession). Keil & Delitzsch's exposition of the whole psalm traces this theme: each generation repeated the pattern of covenant-breaking despite God's faithfulness.

---

## v. 38: *And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them. He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath.*

The Pulpit Commentary notes the allusion to occasions like Exodus 32:10-14, Numbers 14:12-20, and Numbers 16:21, 45-50 — "when God was on the point of destroying the whole people, but relented at the intercession of Moses." It adds: "Yea, many a time turned he his anger away, and did not stir up all his wrath (comp. Judges 2:11-16; 3:8-9; 4:2, 15; 6:1-8, etc.)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Calvin (Reformed) writes: "The reason is assigned why they did not utterly perish. They no doubt deserved to be involved in one common destruction; but it is declared that God mitigated his anger, that some seed of them might remain.… We are not, however, to imagine that he is changeable.… The guilt of men becomes more aggravated, when neither his severity can reform them nor his mercy melt them." He stresses that "the mercy of God, which is an essential attribute of his nature, is here assigned as the reason why he spared his people, to teach us that he was not induced by any other cause but this." (https://ccel.org/study/Ps_78:38-78:39)

The BibleHub topical summary paints a "five-fold portrait of divine mercy: compassionate heart, forgiving grace, protective restraint, patient anger, and limited judgment. Each phrase testifies that God's covenant love outlasts human rebellion." (https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-38.htm)

---

## v. 39: *He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.*

Calvin explains: "Another reason is now brought forward why God had compassion on the people, which is, his unwillingness to try his strength against men who are so constituted as to live only for a short period in this world.… Flesh and spirit are frequently contrasted in the Scriptures… but also when men are called flesh, because there is nothing firm or stable in them." He links this to Psalm 103:13-16: "God is represented as being merciful to us, because he sees that we are like grass, and that we soon wither." (https://ccel.org/study/Ps_78:38-78:39)

The BibleHub summary adds: "The 'passing breeze' pictures the irreversible movement of earthly life toward death… God's purposes extend beyond the grave. The God who knows human frailty has provided redemption and the hope of resurrection through Jesus Christ." (https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-39.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary cross-references Genesis 6:3 ("flesh"), Job 7:7, and James 4:14 ("a vapour that appeareth for a little while, and then vanisheth away"). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 40: *How often they disobeyed Him in the wilderness and grieved Him in the desert!*

This verse opens a new section of the psalm (vv. 40-55). The exclamation "How often!" is a rhetorical cry of lament over Israel's repeated rebellion. Keil & Delitzsch's structure treats vv. 38-72 as the second major part of the psalm, "passing over from the God-tempting unthankfulness of the Israel of the desert to that of the Israel of Canaan." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 41: *Again and again they tested God and provoked the Holy One of Israel.*

Keil & Delitzsch note that the divine title "the Holy One of Israel" (*qedosh Yisrael*) — so characteristic of Isaiah — actually appears first in the Psalms of Asaph. "It cannot surprise us if Asaph is Isaiah's predecessor in the use of the name 'the Holy One of Israel.'" This argues for the psalm's antiquity. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 42: *They did not remember His power — the day He redeemed them from the adversary,*

This introduces the recital of the Egyptian plagues (vv. 43-51). Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that "the plagues of Egypt were God's power directly confronting Egyptian gods: Each plague demonstrated that God was superior to the deities the Egyptians trusted, not merely nature or coincidence." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

---

## v. 43: *when He performed His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan.*

Zoan (Tanis) was an ancient Egyptian city in the north-eastern Nile Delta. Keil & Delitzsch explain it was "the seat of the Hyksos dynasties that ruled in the eastern Delta." They note that the colossal sitting figure of Rameses II in the Berlin Museum "is a contemporary of Moses, who certainly once looked upon this monument, when, as Psalm 78 says, he 'wrought wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.'" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

Kidner (cited by Guzik) adds: "Zoan is better known as Tanis, in the north-east of the Nile Delta, a city which was either identical with Rameses II's capital (Raamses, which the Israelites helped to build: Exodus 1:11) or not many miles from it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

---

## v. 44: *He turned their rivers to blood, and from their streams they could not drink.*

This is the first plague (Exodus 7:19-21). The Pulpit Commentary explains: "'Their rivers' are the many branches of the Nile, some natural, some artificial (Herodotus, 2:17), by which Lower Egypt is traversed. And 'their floods' — i.e., the smaller canals, which diffused the Nile water over the entire land." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 45: *He sent swarms of flies that devoured them, and frogs that devastated them.*

This is the fourth and second plagues respectively. The Pulpit Commentary notes the poet "does not give the plagues in their chronological order, neither regards himself as bound to mention all of them. He omits the third, and reverses the order of the second and fourth." The flies are described as a particular sort — "dog flies" (Kay, Cheyne) or the *Blatta Orientalis* (Canon Cook) — which "devoured them, i.e., preyed upon them, sucking out their life blood." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 46: *He gave their crops to the grasshopper, the fruit of their labor to the locust.*

This is the eighth plague (Exodus 10:14-15). The Pulpit Commentary notes that *khasil*, translated "caterpillar" in the KJV, "is probably either a particular kind of locust, or the locust in one of its stages." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 47: *He killed their vines with hailstones and their sycamore-figs with sleet.*

This is the seventh plague (Exodus 9:23-25). The Pulpit Commentary observes three things: (1) The poet inverts the chronological order (hail preceded locusts). (2) The mention of "vines" is an addition to the Exodus narrative (see also Psalm 105:33), "which may indicate a use of tradition. That vines were cultivated in Egypt is now generally acknowledged." (3) "Sleet" is a variant of the "hail" in the parallel line. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

---

## v. 48: *He abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning.*

The Pulpit Commentary describes the "fire which ran along the ground" (Exodus 9:23) as caused by "electrified clouds of high tension; the highly charged drops of rain meeting the inductively charged earth, and sparking across when within striking distance." It adds: "This is believed to accompany every thunderstorm, though generally invisible to the eye. When exceptionally severe, it would convey the idea of running fire, and would of course be very destructive of life." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm)

Ellicott offers an important textual note: "Some copies read 'pestilence,' which from its association with *resheph*, as in Habakkuk 3:5, a word there denoting some contagious malady (comp. Deuteronomy 32:24; see Note Psalm 76:3), is probably to be preferred here though the authority of the LXX is against it. If so, we must refer this verse to the murrain that came on the cattle." This reflects a text-critical issue where the reading "pestilence" (*deber*) may be original instead of "hail" (*barad*). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm)

Spurgeon (Baptist) reflects on the sobering phrase "gave up": "God usually protects animals from such destruction, but here he withdraws his safeguards and gave them up: may the Lord never give us up. Some read, 'shut up,' and the idea of being abandoned to destructive influences is then before us in another shape." He calls the heart that did not relent under such plagues "harder than adamant." (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php)

---

## Points of Denominational Emphasis

**Reformed (Calvin):** Emphasizes that God's mercy arises purely from His nature, not from human merit. On vv. 38-39, Calvin stresses that "it is solely his own pure and undeserved goodness which induces him to sustain us." The flesh/spirit contrast underlines total depravity and human frailty. (https://ccel.org/study/Ps_78:38-78:39)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Reads the psalm typologically — "Israel in the wilderness acted out, as in a drama, all the story of man's conduct towards his God." He applies the lesson directly to the hearer, urging self-examination: "Ere we condemn them, let us repent of our own wicked forgetfulness." He stresses that unbelief is "the master sin." (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php)

**Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Approaches the psalm with detailed philological and historical precision. They defend its pre-exilic, Asaphic origin against critical scholars, and emphasize the faithfulness of the psalmist's use of the Pentateuchal sources. The divine name "Holy One of Israel" is shown to have early roots in Asaph, not only in Isaiah. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/psalms/78.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Stresses the practical, devotional lesson and the continuing power of God. Guzik cites the story of J. Edwin Orr's 1934 book *Can God—?*, based on Psalm 78:19, as "a remarkable demonstration of the fact that God can prepare a table in the wilderness," and exhorts: "Fetch arguments for faith from the days that have gone… Never say again, 'Can God?' but God can." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/)

**Anglican (Pulpit, Ellicott):** Characteristically balanced — attending to historical context, textual variants, and the natural phenomena behind the miracles (e.g., the electrical explanation for the "fire" in v. 48), while maintaining full reverence for the supernatural character of the events. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm)

---

## Other Views

**Catholic/Orthodox:** The LXX and Vulgate reading "angels' bread" (v. 25) has deeply influenced the liturgical and devotional tradition. Wisdom 16:20, cited by Gill, says: "Instead whereof thou feddest thine own people with angels' food, and didst send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour." This passage from the Deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon is in the Catholic and Orthodox canon and provides the earliest Jewish interpretation of the phrase. The Greek Fathers read the manna typologically as prefiguring the Eucharist — the "bread from heaven" that is truly Christ's body. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/78.htm)

**Modern scholarship (text-critical):** Ellicott's note on v. 48 regarding the variant "pestilence" (possibly referring to the murrain on cattle, Exodus 9:3) represents a text-critical issue. The NET Bible notes (referenced but not accessible in search results) would likely also discuss whether the psalm follows a strict chronological order of the plagues or arranges them for poetic purposes, and whether details like "vines" (v. 47) and the east/south winds (v. 26) represent independent tradition or poetic elaboration.
